Let <MATH_0001> be a topological space and let <MATH_0002>
be a sheaf of rings on <MATH_0003>. We are supposed to
think of the sheaf of rings <MATH_0004> as a sheaf of functions
on <MATH_0005>. And if <MATH_0006> is a ``suitable'' map, then by composition
a function on <MATH_0007> turns into a function on <MATH_0008>.
Thus there should be a natural
<MATH_0009>-map from <MATH_0010> to <MATH_0011>,
see Definition <REF_0001> and
Lemma <REF_0002>.
For a precise example, see
Example <REF_0003> below. Here is the
relevant abstract definition.

A <TEXTITOPEN_0001>ringed space<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> is a pair <MATH_0001> consisting
of a topological space <MATH_0002> and a sheaf of rings <MATH_0003>
on <MATH_0004>. A <TEXTITOPEN_0002>morphism of ringed spaces<TEXTITCLOSE_0002>
<MATH_0005> is a pair
consisting of a continuous map <MATH_0006> and an
<MATH_0007>-map of sheaves of rings
<MATH_0008>.

Of course there are lots of other situations where there is
a canonical morphism of ringed spaces associated to a geometrical
type of morphism. For example, if <MATH_0014>, <MATH_0015> are <MATH_0016>-manifolds
